title: Router Agents
summary: A router agent is a lightweight classifier that reads an incoming request and dispatches it to the right handler — a specialized sub-agent, a specific tool, or a tailored prompt — instead of forcing one giant do-everything agent. The router itself should be cheap and reliable: a small model or even rules, constrained to a fixed set of labels, with a default fallback when it's unsure. Good routing keeps each handler focused and cuts cost, but only if the classification is dependable.

subtopics.title: Why route instead of one big agent
subtopics.explanation: Stuffing every capability, tool, and instruction into a single agent bloats the prompt, confuses the model, and raises cost. A router splits the problem: classify first, then hand off to a focused handler that only knows about its narrow job. Routing is what keeps each handler small and sharp instead of one overloaded generalist.
subtopics.example:
# one-big-agent: every tool + instruction crammed together
# billing + tech + sales tools all in one prompt -> confusion

# router: classify, then dispatch to a FOCUSED handler
label = classify(request)          # 'billing' | 'tech' | 'sales'
handler = HANDLERS[label]          # only that handler's tools/prompt
return handler(request)

subtopics.title: The classifier at the core
subtopics.explanation: The router's job is one decision: map a request to one of a fixed, known set of labels. It can be a small LLM told to output only a label, or plain rules/keywords for simple cases. Constraining the output to a closed label set is what makes routing predictable and easy to validate.

subtopics.title: Dispatch to a sub-agent, tool, or prompt
subtopics.explanation: Once labeled, the request is dispatched to the matching handler: a full sub-agent for complex domains, a single tool call for a narrow action, or just a tailored prompt for a specialized answer. The router doesn't do the work — it picks who does. This separation lets each handler be built and tested independently.

subtopics.title: Keep the router cheap and reliable
subtopics.explanation: The router runs on every request, so it must be fast and cheap — a small model, low temperature, a tight prompt, or rules for obvious cases. Reliability comes from a closed label set and validating the output rather than trusting free text. A cheap, dependable router is the difference between routing saving money and routing becoming its own bottleneck.
subtopics.example:
def classify(request):
    if "refund" in request.lower():     # cheap rule for obvious cases
        return "billing"
    label = small_llm(                   # small model, temp 0
        f"One word label {sorted(LABELS)}: {request}", temperature=0
    ).strip()
    return label if label in LABELS else "unknown"

subtopics.title: Fallback and low-confidence handling
subtopics.explanation: Classifiers get things wrong or hit inputs that fit nothing, so a router needs a default: an 'unknown' route to a general agent, a clarifying question, or a human. When the model can report confidence, low scores should trigger the fallback rather than a confident wrong dispatch. A well-designed fallback is what keeps a misroute from silently sending a user to the wrong place.

foundations.overview: A router agent is an orchestration pattern where a lightweight classifier sits at the front of the system, reads each request, and dispatches it to the appropriate handler — a specialized sub-agent, a specific tool, or a tailored prompt — rather than routing everything through one bloated do-everything agent. The router makes exactly one decision: pick a label from a fixed, closed set. That label maps to a handler that owns the narrow job. Because the router runs on every request, it must be cheap and reliable: a small model at low temperature with a tight prompt, or even plain rules for obvious cases, with its output validated against the known label set. Crucially, no classifier is perfect, so the router needs a fallback — an 'unknown'/general route, a clarifying question, or escalation — for inputs that fit nothing or that the model classifies with low confidence. Done well, routing keeps each handler focused and testable and cuts cost by sending simple requests to cheap paths; done poorly, an unreliable or expensive router becomes its own bottleneck and misroutes users silently.
foundations.formalDefinition: A router agent is a dispatch pattern consisting of a classifier C that maps an input request to a label from a fixed set L (plus a fallback label), and a dispatch table that maps each label to a handler (sub-agent, tool, or prompt). The router validates C's output against L, invokes the matching handler, and routes unrecognized or low-confidence classifications to a default fallback handler.
foundations.whyItMatters: Real systems serve many distinct request types, and one agent trying to handle all of them has a bloated prompt, mixed-up tools, higher cost, and worse accuracy. A router lets you build small, focused, independently testable handlers and send each request to the cheapest capable path, which is a foundational way to scale agent systems in both quality and cost.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a front-desk receptionist at a large office. They don't solve your problem — they figure out in seconds which department you need and send you there. They're fast and cheap (you don't put your best specialist on the desk), they work from a known list of departments, and when someone shows up with a request that fits nothing, they send them to a general help desk rather than guessing wrong.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Customer-support triage routing tickets to billing/technical/account agents; a multi-tool assistant choosing between a search tool, a calculator, and a code interpreter; model routing that sends easy queries to a cheap model and hard ones to a strong model; and intent routers in voice assistants that dispatch to skill-specific handlers.
commonUseCases: Choosing the right tool for a request
Model routing (cheap vs strong model by difficulty)
Intent classification dispatching to skill handlers

commonMisconceptions.myth: The router should also solve the request.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The router makes one decision — which handler — and dispatches. Mixing classification with the actual work bloats it back into the do-everything agent routing was meant to avoid.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A bigger, smarter model makes a better router.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The router runs on every request, so it should be as cheap as possible while staying accurate. A small model, low temperature, or rules for obvious cases usually beat a large model on cost with little accuracy loss.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can dispatch on whatever label the model returns.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Free-text labels drift and hallucinate. Constrain output to a closed set, validate it, and route anything unrecognized to a fallback instead of trusting it blindly.

interactiveExamples.title: A validated classifier with a fallback
interactiveExamples.explanation: A tiny router classifies a request into a closed label set and dispatches to the matching handler, falling back to a general handler for anything it can't confidently label. Validating against the label set is what makes it safe.

code.caption: The closed label set plus a fallback means an unrecognized request goes to a safe general handler instead of a wrong or crashing dispatch.
code.expectedOutput:
billing agent handled it
general agent handled it

interactiveExamples.title: Confidence-aware routing to the fallback
interactiveExamples.explanation: When the classifier can report a confidence score, low scores should route to the fallback rather than committing to a shaky label. This prevents confident-but-wrong dispatches on ambiguous inputs.

code.caption: A confidence threshold turns a shaky guess into a clarifying fallback instead of a confident misroute — cheap insurance against sending users to the wrong place.
code.expectedOutput:
routed to billing
clarify: could you tell me more?

codeLab.title: Build a validated router with confidence fallback
codeLab.instructions: Implement route(request, classify, handlers, threshold=0.6, fallback=...). classify(request) returns a dict {"label": str, "confidence": float}. handlers is a dict mapping label -> callable(request) -> str. fallback is a callable(request) -> str. Your router must: (1) call classify; (2) route to the fallback if the returned label is NOT a key in handlers OR the confidence is below threshold; (3) otherwise call the matching handler with the request and return its result. Never call a handler for an unvalidated or low-confidence label. Complete route so the harness passes.
hints: Read both label and confidence out of the classify result before deciding anything.
Use a single guard: if the label isn't a handlers key OR confidence < threshold, return fallback(request).
Only index handlers[label] after that guard passes, so an unknown label can never raise a KeyError.

checkpoints.prompt: What is a router agent's single responsibility?
options: Solve the request end to end
Classify the request and dispatch it to the right handler
checkpoints.explanation: A router makes one decision — which handler (sub-agent, tool, or prompt) should take the request — and dispatches to it. Doing the actual work is the handler's job; mixing that back into the router recreates the do-everything agent.

checkpoints.prompt: This router can crash or misroute. What's the flaw?
checkpoints.code:
label = classify(request)          # returns free-text label
return HANDLERS[label](request)    # dispatch directly
options: The label is dispatched without validating it against the known set or handling 'unknown', so a hallucinated label raises KeyError or misroutes
checkpoints.explanation: Trusting a free-text label directly means a hallucinated or unexpected label indexes a missing key (KeyError) or sends the user to the wrong handler. Validate against a closed set and route unknowns to a fallback.

checkpoints.prompt: What does this confidence-gated router return?
checkpoints.explanation: Confidence 0.5 is below the 0.6 threshold, so the router returns 'fallback' instead of committing to the shaky 'tech' label — the confidence gate prevents a low-confidence misroute.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the guard so unknown labels never reach a handler.
checkpoints.explanation: `if label not in handlers` sends any label without a registered handler to the fallback, so a hallucinated or out-of-set label can never cause a KeyError or a wrong dispatch.

theory.question: What is a router agent and why use one instead of a single do-everything agent?
theory.directAnswer: A router agent is a lightweight classifier that reads each request, picks a label from a fixed set, and dispatches to the matching handler — a sub-agent, tool, or tailored prompt. You use it instead of one big agent because cramming every tool and instruction into a single prompt bloats it, confuses the model, raises cost, and lowers accuracy; routing lets you build small, focused, independently testable handlers and send each request to the cheapest capable path.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A dispatch pattern: a classifier at the front mapping requests to labels, and a table mapping labels to handlers.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Because real systems serve many distinct request types that a single overloaded agent handles poorly and expensively.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The router classifies into a closed label set, validates the label, invokes the matching handler, and routes anything unrecognized or low-confidence to a fallback.

theory.whyImportant: Routing is a foundational way to scale agent systems in both quality and cost, and it's a common interview probe for whether you decompose problems instead of building monoliths.
theory.realWorldExample: A support system routes each ticket to a billing, technical, or account sub-agent; each handler has only its own tools and prompt, so it's simpler and more accurate than one agent juggling all three.

followUps.question: Should the router ever answer the request itself?
followUps.answer: No — its one job is choosing the handler. Doing the work in the router recreates the bloated do-everything agent routing was meant to eliminate.

followUps.question: What can a handler be?
followUps.answer: Anything that does the work: a full sub-agent for complex domains, a single tool for a narrow action, or just a specialized prompt for a tailored answer.

theory.question: How do you keep a router cheap and reliable, and why does the fallback matter?
theory.directAnswer: Keep it cheap by using a small model at low temperature with a tight prompt (or plain rules for obvious cases) since the router runs on every request; keep it reliable by constraining output to a closed label set and validating it rather than trusting free text. The fallback matters because no classifier is perfect: unrecognized inputs and low-confidence guesses should route to a default (general agent, clarifying question, or human) so a misclassification never silently sends a user to the wrong handler or crashes on an unknown label.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The cost/reliability engineering of the classification-and-dispatch step plus its safety net for uncertain inputs.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Because the router is on the hot path of every request, and classifiers occasionally hallucinate labels or face inputs that fit nothing.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Use the cheapest accurate classifier, restrict and validate its output against known labels, gate on confidence when available, and dispatch anything invalid or uncertain to a fallback handler.

theory.whyImportant: An expensive router negates routing's cost savings, and a router without a fallback turns every misclassification into a silent wrong answer — both are common production failures.
theory.realWorldExample: A team replaced a large-model router with a small model at temperature 0 plus keyword shortcuts, cutting routing cost sharply; an 'unknown' fallback to a general agent caught the rare out-of-set request instead of crashing.

followUps.question: When are rules better than an LLM for routing?
followUps.answer: When labels are cleanly signaled by keywords or metadata — rules are free, deterministic, and instant; reserve the LLM for genuinely ambiguous requests.

followUps.question: How do you use confidence in routing?
followUps.answer: If the classifier reports confidence, route below-threshold results to the fallback or a clarifying question rather than committing to a shaky label.

scenario.question: Your router misclassifies about 8% of requests, sometimes to a non-existent label that crashes the dispatch. How would you diagnose and harden it?
scenario.directAnswer: First stop the crashes by validating every label against the closed set and dispatching unknowns to a fallback so a bad label can never KeyError. Then diagnose the 8%: log request, predicted label, and (if available) confidence, and inspect the confusion pairs to find which categories blur. Fix the top causes with clearer label definitions and few-shot examples in the router prompt, add cheap keyword rules for obvious cases, gate low-confidence predictions to the fallback or a clarifying question, and track routing accuracy as a live metric.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A reliability-hardening problem for the classification-and-dispatch step, covering both crashes and misroutes.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Unvalidated labels crash dispatch, and ambiguous or poorly defined categories cause the model to confuse neighboring labels.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Validate and fall back to eliminate crashes, log and build a confusion analysis to find the dominant misroute pairs, then improve label clarity, add examples/rules, and use confidence gating — measuring accuracy continuously to catch regressions.

scenario.whyImportant: It shows both defensive engineering (never trust the label) and a metrics-driven approach to improving classification, which is exactly how production routers are hardened.
scenario.realWorldExample: Logs revealed most errors were billing-vs-sales confusion on pricing questions; sharper label definitions plus a few examples and a confidence-gated fallback cut misroutes well below 8% and eliminated the crashes entirely.

followUps.question: Why validate the label even after improving accuracy?
followUps.answer: Accuracy is never 100% and models can still emit an out-of-set token; validation plus fallback is a permanent safety boundary, not a temporary patch.

followUps.question: How would you catch a future regression fast?
followUps.answer: Alert on the live routing-accuracy metric (and fallback rate) per model version so a prompt or model change that reintroduces confusion is caught early.

coding.question: Implement a router that classifies a request, validates the label against a closed set, gates on confidence, and dispatches to a handler or a fallback.
coding.thoughtProcess: The router's contract is one decision plus a safe dispatch. I read the classifier's label and confidence, then apply a single guard: if the label isn't a known handler key or the confidence is below threshold, I route to the fallback. Only after that guard do I index the handlers table, so an unknown label can never raise a KeyError and a shaky guess never reaches a real handler.
lineByLine: The router takes the classifier, the handler table, a fallback, and a confidence threshold as explicit dependencies.
It reads the predicted label and confidence, defaulting confidence to 1.0 if the classifier doesn't report one.
The single guard validates the label against the closed handler set and enforces the confidence threshold.
Any unknown label or low-confidence prediction is routed to the fallback instead of a handler.
Only after the guard passes do we index handlers[label], so a bad label can never raise a KeyError.
The __main__ demo shows a confident 'billing' dispatch and a low-confidence guess falling back to the general agent.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) dispatch after the classify call, which dominates cost.

followUps.question: How would you add cheap keyword shortcuts?
followUps.answer: Check obvious keywords before calling the model classifier and return the label directly, reserving the model for ambiguous requests to cut cost.

followUps.question: How would you observe router health?
followUps.answer: Log request, chosen label, confidence, and whether it fell back; track routing accuracy and fallback rate per model version to catch regressions.

keyTakeaways: A router agent classifies each request and dispatches it to the right handler (sub-agent, tool, or prompt) instead of one bloated do-everything agent.
The router makes one decision only — pick a label from a closed set — so keep the actual work in the handlers.
It runs on every request, so make it cheap: a small model at low temperature, a tight prompt, or plain rules for obvious cases.
Constrain output to a known label set and validate it; never dispatch a free-text label you can't verify.
Always provide a fallback for unknown or low-confidence classifications so a misroute never crashes or silently sends the user to the wrong place.
